title: Confessions, Book 8: a sustained reading

objectives.can: Read the garden scene of Confessions 8 with only occasional help and follow its narrative and its argument.

explanation.summary: The last six sections of the garden scene (Confessions 8.25 to 8.30) are among the best-known pages of Latin Christian literature. This lesson names the features that carry the story and the argument, then sends you into the text: the tenses that tell the tale, the reported speech, the commands, and the quotations from Scripture that Augustine weaves into his own sentences.

sections.heading: The tenses that tell the story
body: Augustine uses the imperfect for the long struggle and the perfect for the turning points. In 8.25 the imperfects pile up: *iam paene faciebam et non faciebam nec relabebar tamen in pristina, sed de proximo stabam et respirabam*, 'I was all but doing it and was not doing it, and I was not slipping back, but I stood close by and drew breath'. Nothing is finished; the verbs hang in the middle of the action.

In 8.29 the story moves. *Dicebam haec et flebam* is imperfect, the continuing grief. Then the present, *ecce audio uocem*, brings the reader into the moment of hearing (grammarians call this a historic present). The perfects follow in rapid order: *coepi*, *surrexi*, *arripui*, *aperui et legi*. Short perfects in a row are a quick sequence of acts.

The pluperfect looks back: *audieram enim de Antonio* gives the earlier event that explains the present one, and *ibi enim posueram codicem apostoli* tells where he had left the book. Whenever you see a pluperfect, ask what earlier event it supplies.

sections.heading: Reported speech and thought
body: Sections 8.29 and 8.30 are full of reported thought. *cogitare coepi, utrumnam solerent pueri in aliquo genere ludendi cantitare tale aliquid* is an indirect question: he began to think whether children were accustomed to sing something of the sort in some game. The imperfect subjunctive *solerent* follows a past main verb, as in the earlier lessons on sequence.

*nihil aliud interpretans diuinitus mihi iuberi, nisi ut aperirem codicem et legerem* has two layers. *iuberi* is a passive infinitive in an indirect statement after *interpretans*, 'understanding that I was being ordered', and *ut aperirem … et legerem* names the order. And *audieram … de Antonio, quod … admonitus fuerit, tamquam sibi diceretur quod legebatur* reports what he had heard, with *quod* and the subjunctive; *tamquam sibi diceretur* says Antony took the words as if they were addressed to him. The mood marks the report; you can drop it in English.
In 8.30 *petit uidere quid legissem* is an indirect question in the pluperfect subjunctive, 'what I had read', and *ignorabam quid sequeretur*, 'I did not know what followed', is another.

sections.heading: Direct speech inside the narrative: commands and prohibitions
body: Within the story people speak, and the speech is direct. The child's voice says *tolle lege*, two imperatives, 'take up, read'. In 8.27 Continence says *proice te in eum, noli metuere*, 'throw yourself on him, do not be afraid'; *noli* with an infinitive is the ordinary Latin for a negative command. In 8.25 Augustine says to himself *ecce modo fiat, modo fiat*: *fiat* is a subjunctive of exhortation, 'let it be now, let it be now'.

The quotation of Paul ends in a prohibition of another kind: *carnis prouidentiam ne feceritis in concupiscentiis*, 'make no provision for the flesh in its desires'. The perfect subjunctive with *ne* is an old form of prohibition. Beside it stands the positive command *induite dominum Iesum Christum*, 'put on the Lord Jesus Christ'.

sections.heading: Scripture in Augustine's sentences
body: Augustine seldom marks a quotation. The passages to know here are the words that Antony heard, *uade, uende omnia, quae habes, da pauperibus … et ueni, sequere me*, which are the words of the Gospel; the lines from the psalms that he prays in tears (*usquequo, domine, irasceris in finem?*, *ne memor fueris iniquitatum nostrarum antiquarum*); and the verse of Paul's letter to the Romans that he reads when he opens the book.

Augustine says plainly that his prayer in 8.28 is in the sense of these words and not in these words: *non quidem his uerbis, sed in hac sententia multa dixi tibi*. A quotation is a way to speak; it does not stop the sentence. The Latin of the Bible he quotes is not always the Latin of the Vulgate; he knew other Latin versions.

sections.heading: The scene in six steps, and its argument
body: 8.25: he struggles and puts things off: *modo*, 'now', and the habit that holds him. 8.26: the old loves, *nugae nugarum*, tug at his flesh-coloured garment and ask *dimittisne nos?*, 'will you send us away?'. 8.27: Continence appears as a woman with her children, laughing at his hesitation, and tells him to throw himself on God. 8.28: he rises, goes alone under a fig tree and weeps. 8.29: the child's voice, the book, the verse. 8.30: Alypius reads on, takes the next words to himself, and they go to Monica.

The argument underneath is the one of the whole book: a divided will cannot be healed by command or by effort alone. Augustine's account is that the will is turned by a word it did not choose. A good reader sees how the grammar serves that account: the imperfects of delay, the sudden present of the voice, the pluperfect of the earlier story, the imperatives that cut through the dialogue.

misunderstandings: The historic present is not a mistake of tense. It is a choice, and in 8.29 it marks the moment of hearing.
A pluperfect does not mean the action is remote; it means that it comes before the story's present moment. *audieram … de Antonio* is the story that moves Augustine now.
Do not read every subjunctive as a wish or a doubt. In *utrumnam solerent* it follows from the indirect question, and in *ne feceritis* it is a prohibition.
Biblical language in a sentence does not make it a quotation of an exact text. Augustine himself warns that what he prays is in the sense of the psalm and not in its words.

deeper.heading: Tolle lege
body: Augustine says that he did not know whether the child's voice was a boy's or a girl's, and he does not claim to know what game it came from: *quasi pueri an puellae, nescio*. He also considers that it may be a game and finds no such song in his memory. His reading of it as a divine command is his interpretation, and the narrative marks it as such with the word *interpretans*. A reader may leave open what happened in the garden and still follow what Augustine says happened.

examples.analysis: *Dicebam* and *flebam* are imperfect: he was speaking and weeping. *audio* is a present that brings the moment of hearing before the reader's eyes. *coepi* and *surrexi* are perfects: he began, he rose. The change of tense from the imperfect to the present and then to a run of perfects carries the story from the long grief to the sudden action.

examples.analysis: *dicebam* introduces his speech to himself: *ecce modo fiat, modo fiat*. *fiat* is a present subjunctive of exhortation, 'let it be done now'. The verbs that follow, *faciebam*, *relabebar*, *stabam*, *respirabam*, are all imperfect: they describe what was going on, not an event, and the double *faciebam … non faciebam* shows the doing and the not-doing held together.

examples.analysis: *inridebat* is imperfect: she laughed at him, as a habit of the scene. *quasi diceret* is 'as if she were saying': Continence does not speak aloud, and the imperfect subjunctive after *quasi* marks the speech as imagined. *proice* is an imperative. *subtrahet* and *excipiet* are futures: He will not withdraw himself, he will receive you. *ut cadas* is a clause of purpose or result, 'so that you fall'.

examples.analysis: The verse Augustine reads is built of three pairs of nouns, each introduced by *non in*: *comisationibus et ebrietatibus*, *cubilibus et inpudicitiis*, *contentione et aemulatione*, and then turns at *sed* to a positive command, *induite dominum Iesum Christum*. The last clause, with *prouidentiam*, is a prohibition (*ne feceritis*) that closes the series. The balance of the pairs against the single command is part of what the verse does.

examples.analysis: *petit* is a present: Alypius asks. *quid legissem* is an indirect question with a pluperfect subjunctive, 'what I had read'. *ignorabam quid sequeretur* is another, the imperfect subjunctive of what was following. Then the narrative states what followed with *sequebatur* and a quotation. *rettulit* is a perfect: he referred the words to himself.

practice.prompt: *Dicebam haec et flebam amarissima contritione cordis mei. et ecce audio uocem de diuina domo …* Why does Augustine pass from the imperfect to the present with *audio*?

quoted.title: Confessions
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

options: Because he is now writing in the present day.
The present is a mistake of the copyist.
The present is a vivid way of telling the moment of hearing, after the long continuing grief of the imperfects.
practice.explain: *Dicebam* and *flebam* are imperfects of continuing action. *ecce audio* is a historic present: the same time in the story, told as if it were happening. It marks the turning point. It is not a subjunctive, and there is no ground for suspecting a mistake.

options: It shows that the story ends here.
It is a wish that he might hear.
It gives an earlier event that explains the present moment: he had heard about Antony before.
practice.explain: The pluperfect looks back from the narrative's present. Augustine had heard the story of Antony from Ponticianus, and that earlier hearing explains why he now expects the book to speak to him. *enim* ('for') confirms that the sentence gives a reason.

options: A direct question with the verb in the indicative.
An indirect question: whether children were accustomed to sing something of the sort in some game.
A purpose clause: he thought so that children might sing.
practice.explain: *utrumnam* means 'whether', and the verb *solerent* is imperfect subjunctive after the past *coepi*, the normal pattern for an indirect question in secondary sequence. There is no antecedent, so the clause is not a relative one.

practice.prompt: *sed induite dominum Iesum Christum et carnis prouidentiam ne feceritis in concupiscentiis.* What are *induite* and *ne feceritis*?

options: Two commands, both with the imperative.
A command (*induite*) and a prohibition (*ne feceritis*), both addressed to the readers of Paul's letter.
practice.explain: *induite* is a plural imperative. *ne feceritis* is a perfect subjunctive with *ne*, an old way of forbidding. Together they give the positive and the negative sides of the same exhortation.

options: A subjunctive of exhortation, 'let it be done now'.
practice.explain: *fiat* is the present subjunctive of *fio*, and a main-clause subjunctive of this kind urges or wishes: 'let it happen now'. Augustine is speaking to himself and putting off the change, as the repeated *modo* shows.

check.prompt: *iam paene faciebam et non faciebam nec relabebar tamen in pristina, sed de proximo stabam et respirabam.* Why are the verbs imperfect?

quoted.title: Confessions
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

options: They are all in indirect speech.
They report a single act that finished at once.
They describe a continued, unfinished state: the struggle is going on and nothing is yet done.
check.explain: The imperfect shows an action going on or attempted. *iam paene faciebam* means 'I was all but doing it', and the four imperfects together hold the reader inside the delay. A single completed act would be a perfect, which comes with the change at *surrexi* and *legi*.

check.prompt: *Retinebant nugae nugarum et uanitates uanitantium, antiquae amicae meae, et succutiebant uestem meam carneam et submurmurabant: dimittisne nos?* Who speaks, and what is the form *dimittisne*?

quoted.title: Confessions
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

options: The old loves, trifles of trifles, personified as friends; *dimittisne* is a question marked by *-ne*.
check.explain: The subjects of *retinebant*, *succutiebant* and *submurmurabant* are *nugae* and *uanitates*, which Augustine calls *antiquae amicae meae*. What they murmur is a question with the enclitic *-ne*: 'will you send us away?'. The speakers are not people in the scene.

check.prompt: *et inridebat me inrisione hortatoria, quasi diceret: tu non poteris quod isti, quod istae?* What does *quasi diceret* tell the reader?

quoted.title: Confessions

options: That the verb *diceret* is a command.
That the speech is imagined: she laughed as if she were saying it.
That Continence spoke these words aloud to everyone.
That the words are a quotation from Scripture.
check.explain: *quasi* with the subjunctive introduces a comparison with something supposed: 'as if she said'. The figure of Continence smiles and speaks only in Augustine's mind, and the same *quasi diceret* is repeated later in the section for her second speech.

check.prompt: *proice te in eum, noli metuere; non se subtrahet, ut cadas: proice te securus, excipiet et sanabit te.* How are the commands and the reassurance related?

quoted.title: Confessions
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

options: *noli metuere* is a statement that he does not fear.
*proice* and *noli metuere* are a command and a negative command; *non se subtrahet* and *excipiet et sanabit* are future promises that give the ground for them.
*ut cadas* is a command to fall.
check.explain: *proice* is an imperative, and *noli* with an infinitive is the ordinary negative command. The futures *subtrahet*, *excipiet*, *sanabit* say what God will do, and so they give the reason for obeying. *ut cadas* tells what he will not allow: 'so that you fall'.

check.prompt: *et ut totum effunderem cum uocibus suis, surrexi ab Alypio.* What does *ut effunderem* express?

options: A condition: if he poured out.
A purpose: he rose in order to pour out the whole of it with his weeping.
An indirect question: whether he should pour out his tears.
A result: he rose and as a result poured everything out.
check.explain: *ut* with the imperfect subjunctive after the perfect *surrexi* gives the aim of rising: he left Alypius so as to weep freely. The next lines say that solitude seemed better for weeping.

check.prompt: *non quidem his uerbis, sed in hac sententia multa dixi tibi: et tu, domine, usquequo? usquequo, domine, irasceris in finem?* What does Augustine say about the prayer that follows?

quoted.title: Confessions

options: That the words are exactly the ones he spoke in the garden.
That the prayer was written by Alypius.
That he prayed in the sense of these words, drawn from the psalms, though not in just these words.
That the prayer was said in silence by Monica.
check.explain: *non quidem his uerbis, sed in hac sententia* means 'not in these words, but in this sense'. Augustine gives the psalm language as the sense of what he said. A reader should not take the quoted lines as a transcript.

check.prompt: *audieram enim de Antonio … tamquam sibi diceretur quod legebatur: uade, uende omnia, quae habes, da pauperibus et habebis thesaurum in caelis; et ueni, sequere me.* Whose words are *uade, uende …*, and who takes them as spoken to himself?

quoted.title: Confessions

options: They are the words of Alypius to Augustine.
They are the words of the child's voice to Augustine.
They are words that Augustine invented for Antony.
They are words of the Gospel, from a reading on which Antony happened to come, and Antony took them as spoken to himself.
check.explain: *tamquam sibi diceretur* shows that Antony took the reading as addressed to himself. The words are the Gospel imperatives. The child's voice is only *tolle lege*, and the passage from Paul is the one that Augustine reads, not Antony.

check.prompt: In *non in comisationibus et ebrietatibus, non in cubilibus et inpudicitiis, non in contentione et aemulatione, sed induite dominum Iesum Christum*, how is the quotation built?

options: Three pairs of things to avoid, each with *non in*, set against the one positive command *induite …*.
A single question with four parts.
A report of what Alypius said.
Four commands, all in the imperative.
check.explain: The negatives *non in … et …* come three times, and *sed* turns to the command. The long run of negatives makes the single command stand out when it comes.

check.prompt: *petit uidere quid legissem: ostendi, et adtendit etiam ultra quam ego legeram. et ignorabam quid sequeretur. sequebatur autem: infirmum uero in fide recipe. quod ille ad se rettulit …* What happens in this passage?

options: Alypius takes the book and runs away.
Alypius asks to see what Augustine read, reads on beyond that point, and takes the next words to himself; Augustine had not known them.
Augustine reads the next verse aloud and Alypius is silent.
Monica reads the verse after the other two have left.
check.explain: *petit uidere* and *ostendi* are the request and the showing. *adtendit etiam ultra quam ego legeram* means that Alypius read beyond the place at which Augustine stopped, and *ignorabam quid sequeretur* says that Augustine did not know the words that came next. *quod ille ad se rettulit* is the application to himself.

reading.reference: Augustine of Hippo, Confessions 8.25 – Augustine of Hippo, Confessions 8.30
reading.why: The climax of the garden scene, from the delay (*modo et modo*), through the old loves and Continence, to the tears, the voice, the book and the verse of Paul. It is narrative with imperfects and perfects, reported thought, direct speech and quotation from Scripture, and it calls on everything in this unit.
